item.title: About Us
item.description:
About Us

History

Fernglen, named after the family home in England, was purchased by the Fisher family in July 1888. The property consisted of a mix of native bush and scrubland. Part of the scrubland was cleared for market gardening and grazing, and the native bush area was interplanted with pōhutukawa, rimu and kahikatea in the early 1920s.

Fernglen has been used for education and research since the 1920s by such people as T.F. Cheeseman of the Auckland Museum, Professor Lancaster of the Auckland University, H.B. Dobbie, Frank Fisher and his son William and by Muriel Fisher. More about the history of Fernglen

item.title: Contact Us / Donate
item.description:
Contact Us

Fernglen Native Plant Gardens are located at:

36 Kauri Road (between house numbers 34 and 48)
Birkenhead
Auckland
New Zealand
021 236 5800

Fernglen is owned by the Auckland Council. Education and events are operated through the Fernglen Native Plant Gardens educational committee and trust.

Visitors to Fernglen are most welcome throughout the week during daylight hours. Gardening associations and similar groups may wish to inform Fernglen of their group’s visit by emailing at fernglen.nz@gmail.com or telephoning 021 236 5800.

item.title: Events
item.description:
Events

The Fernglen education room is popular to hire for children’s birthday parties, meetings, yoga and more. The room is available for hire. For more please email: fernglen.nz@gmail.com

Verran School memorial plaque for Muriel Fisher

Verran Primary School has been involved with the garden for many years and planted a kōwhai tree in the rock garden area in Muriel’s honour when she died in 2012. On 23rd May a group of students and teachers mounted a memorial plaque near the kōwhai in memory of Muriel Fisher.

item.title: History
item.description:
Fernglen History

Fernglen is named after the family home in England. It was purchased by Frank Fisher in July 1888. The property consisted of a mix of native bush and scrubland. Part of the scrubland was cleared for market gardening and grazing, and the native bush area was interplanted with pōhutukawa, rimu and kahikatea in the early 1920s.

Frank Fisher grew tomatoes, and ferns of which he would sell the fronds to the Auckland florists. He was a skilled propagator and passed on his knowledge to his son Bill.

item.title: Native Fauna
item.description:
Fernglen Native Fauna

Fernglen is home to native birds, insects, reptiles, glow worms and fresh water fish.

Birds commonly found at Fernglen

  • Tūī
  • Piwakawaka fantail
  • Kererū wood pigeon
  • Riroriro grey warbler
  • Ruru morepork
  • Pipiwharauroa or shining cuckoo in spring and summer
  • Tauhou silvereye
  • Kotare kingfisher
  • Isolated sightings of Kākā

Other native fauna

  • Wētā
  • Skinks
  • Gecko
  • Glow worms

Friends of Fernglen Newsletters

As Fernglen grows, it needs continued support from interested members of the community. One way to show your support is by joining the mailing list and receive newsletters every quarter. Fernglen is reliant on the community to assist with working bees and financial support to assist in maintaining and growing its rare plant collection. If you would like to receive news from Fernglen please email Fernglen

item.title: Visits
item.description:
Visits to Fernglen

Fernglen Native Plant Gardens has always been a place of education. This began way back in the 1900s with the notable T.F. Cheeseman of the Auckland Museum, Professor Lancaster of the Auckland University, H.B. Dobbie. Frank Fisher and Bill and into the 2000s, Muriel Fisher, shared their extensive knowledge of rare and endangered plants.

Today this education continues with very knowledgeable members of the Fernglen Gardens Educational committee and trust, and Landscape Solutions, Fernglen Curator Deborah, who works in the gardens on Tuesdays and Fridays.

item.title: Walks
item.description:
Fernglen Garden and Bush Walk

Fernglen has well maintained walking tracks that provide an excellent opportunity to observe many interesting species. As you enter the gates to Fernglen there is a kiosk that provides general information about New Zealand flora, a history of Fernglen with notes on the different groups of plants to be seen and a plan of the region drawn to scale. A self-guided tour is available. Take an instructional guide from a tray in the kiosk. Follow the directions on the instruction guide to marked numbers within the garden, each one tells a little about the 26 specific plants/trees of interest. Within the walk is an active water way running over mountain rocks, inspired by Muriel Fisher’s many walks in the Aoraki/Mt Cook region.
